A basic torch from a supermarket or pound shop costs a few pounds and does the job.
Your phone torch will do for a short power cut, but it runs the battery down. Avoid candles: they cause fires in power cuts.
If you have a car, its radio works in a power cut. Only run the engine outside, never in a garage.
A basic battery radio is the cheapest kind. Wind-up ones cost more.
Keep your phone charged above half when bad weather is forecast. That costs nothing.
If you have a car, a car charger works too. Small power banks are the cheapest.
Use what you already have: duvets, coats, hats and thick socks. Put them where you can find them in the dark.
Charity shops sell blankets and coats for very little.
Start with what's already in your cupboard: plasters, paracetamol, any bandages. Put them in one box.
Supermarket own-brand kits cost much less than branded ones.
You probably have most of this already: bin bags, a bucket, hand gel and wet wipes. Put them together.
Own-brand wet wipes and hand gel are fine.
Any bag will do: an old rucksack or a strong carrier bag by the door. What's inside matters, not the bag.
Supermarkets sell basic tin openers for a pound or two.
Or choose ring-pull tins when you shop.
Buy one extra tin or bag of their usual food with your normal shop.
